text: Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming, and with him four hundred men. So he divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two servant women.
He put the servant women and their children first, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last.
He himself went on ahead of them, bowing to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him; he threw his arms around his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
Then Esau looked up and saw the women and the children, and he asked, "Who are these with you?" Jacob answered, "The children God has graciously given your servant."
Then the servant women came forward with their children and bowed down.
Leah also came forward with her children, and they bowed down. Last of all Joseph and Rachel came forward and bowed down.
Esau asked, "What was the meaning of all those droves I met?" Jacob said, "To find favor in my lord's eyes."
But Esau said, "I have plenty, my brother. Keep what is yours."
Jacob replied, "No, please—if I have found favor in your eyes, then accept this gift from my hand. For to see your face is like seeing the face of God, now that you have received me so kindly.
"Please take the blessing I have brought you, for God has been gracious to me, and I have all I need." So Jacob urged him, and he accepted it.

versions.text: Please take the blessing I have brought you, for God has been gracious to me, and I have all I need." So Jacob urged him, and he accepted it.
versions.explanation: Jacob's speech begun in verse 10 continues here, but the verse opens without a quotation mark while it closes with one. Adding the opening quotation mark makes the continued speech clear for readers and for those reading aloud.

text: Then Esau said, "Let us set out and be on our way, and I will travel alongside you."

But Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are frail, and that the flocks and herds are nursing their young and are my charge. If they are driven hard for even a single day, all the flocks will die.

versions.text: But Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are frail, and that the flocks and herds have young with them. If they are driven hard for even a single day, all the animals will die.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew specifies כָּל־הַצֹּאן, "all the flock(s)," echoing the flocks named earlier in the verse. "All the animals" broadens the term unnecessarily and loses the deliberate repetition.

versions.text: But Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are frail, and that the flocks and herds have young with them. If they are driven hard for even a single day, all the flocks will die.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew עָלוֹת עָלָי carries two ideas: the animals are nursing (עָלוֹת, ewes and cows with suckling young) and they are Jacob's responsibility (עָלָי, literally "upon me"). The present rendering conveys the first but drops the second, which is what grounds Jacob's plea about pace. The existing wording is a defensible paraphrase, so it remains a legitimate alternative.

text: Let my lord go on ahead of his servant, and I will move along slowly, at the pace of the herds before me and the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir."
Esau said, "Then let me leave some of my men with you." "Why do that?" Jacob answered. "Only let me find favor in my lord's eyes."
So that day Esau started back on his way to Seir.
Jacob, however, journeyed on to Succoth, where he built himself a house and made shelters for his livestock. That is why the place is called Succoth.
After coming from Paddan Aram, Jacob arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan and camped within sight of the city.
For a hundred pieces of silver he bought from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, the plot of ground where he had pitched his tent.[fn]

versions.text: For a hundred pieces of silver he bought from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, the plot of ground where he had pitched his tent.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew term is qesitah, an ancient unit of weight or currency of unknown value. A brief footnote such as "Hebrew a hundred qesitah, a unit of unknown value" would help readers without disturbing the smooth reading of the text.

text: There he set up an altar and called it El Elohe Israel—God, the God of Israel.
